slides.title: Start with something easy
slides.text: Here is the graph of a function $f$. Find the point on the graph above $x = 2$ and read its height.
slides.hint: Go to 2 on the x-axis, move straight up to the graph, then read the height on the y-axis.

slides.title: Now walk toward it
slides.text: Forget the point at $x = 2$ for a moment. Drag the slider so $x$ gets close to 2 from the left, then from the right. Watch the height $f(x)$.
slides.after: From both sides, the height closes in on 3.

slides.text: As $x$ gets close to 2, what height is the graph heading toward?
slides.hint: Think back to the slider. What number was $f(x)$ closing in on?

slides.title: That height is the limit
slides.text:
The height the graph is heading toward as $x$ gets close to 2 is called the **limit**. We write

$lim[x->2] f(x) = 3$

and say “the limit of $f(x)$ as $x$ approaches 2 is 3.”

So far the limit and the value $f(2)$ are the same number. That will not always be true.

slides.title: Take the point away
slides.text: This graph has an open circle at $x = 2$. An open circle means the function has no value there. What is $f(2)$?
slides.hint: An open circle is a missing point. Is there any filled point above $x = 2$?
slides.explain: There is no point on the graph above $x = 2$, so $f(2)$ is undefined.

slides.text: The point is gone. Drag toward $x = 2$ from both sides anyway. Where is the graph heading?
slides.after: Still closing in on 3, even though the graph never gets there.

slides.text: $f(2)$ is undefined. What is the limit?
slides.hint: The limit asks where the graph is heading, not what happens at $x = 2$ itself.
slides.explain: The graph heads to height 3 from both sides. The missing point does not matter.

slides.title: Move the point somewhere else
slides.text: Now there is a filled point at $(2, 5)$, away from the rest of the graph. What is $f(2)$?
slides.hint: The filled point is the actual value. How high is it?
slides.explain: The filled point above $x = 2$ is at height 5.

slides.text: Same graph. What is the limit as $x$ approaches 2?
slides.hint: Ignore the filled point. Follow the line toward $x = 2$ from each side.
slides.explain: The line still heads to height 3. The filled point at height 5 is $f(2)$, not the limit.

slides.title: The big idea
slides.text:
Three graphs gave three different answers for $f(2)$: 3, undefined, and 5. The limit was 3 every time.

**A limit is the height the graph looks like it is heading toward. It does not matter whether the function actually gets there.**

slides.title: Quick check
slides.hint: Think about the last graph. $f(2)$ was 5 there. What was the limit?
slides.explain: The value at the point and the limit can be different numbers.

slides.title: When the two sides disagree
slides.text: This graph jumps at $x = 2$. Drag toward 2 from the left, then from the right. Do you get the same height?
slides.after: From the left the height closes in on 1. From the right it closes in on 3.

slides.text: Coming from the **left**, what height is the graph heading toward? This is the left-hand limit, written $lim[x->2^-] f(x)$.
slides.hint: Stay on the piece to the left of $x = 2$ and follow it toward 2.
slides.explain: The left piece heads to height 1.

slides.text: Coming from the **right**, what height is the graph heading toward? This is the right-hand limit, written $lim[x->2^+] f(x)$.
slides.hint: Stay on the piece to the right of $x = 2$ and follow it back toward 2.
slides.explain: The right piece heads to the open circle at height 3.

slides.title: One-sided limits
slides.text:
$lim[x->2^-] f(x) = 1$ is the **left-hand limit**: $x$ approaches 2 through values less than 2.

$lim[x->2^+] f(x) = 3$ is the **right-hand limit**: $x$ approaches 2 through values greater than 2.

The ordinary two-sided limit exists only when both sides head to the **same** height.
The left side heads to 1 and the right side heads to 3. What is the two-sided limit?
slides.hint: The two sides disagree. When that happens the limit does not exist. Use the DNE button.
slides.explain: The sides disagree, so the limit does not exist (DNE). Each one-sided limit still exists.

slides.title: Put it together
slides.text: $lim[x->4^-] f(x) = 6$ and $lim[x->4^+] f(x) = 6$, but $f(4) = 1$. What is $lim[x->4] f(x)$?
slides.hint: Both sides agree. Does the value $f(4)$ change where the graph is heading?
slides.explain: Both sides head to 6, so the limit is 6. The value $f(4) = 1$ does not affect it.

slides.text: A limit exists at $x = a$ only when the left-hand and right-hand limits are ___. The value of $f(a)$ ___ matter.
slides.hint: When do the two sides give one answer? And did the filled point ever change a limit?
slides.explain: Both sides must agree, and the value at the point is irrelevant.

slides.title: Practice unlocked
slides.text:
You now know the three things this unit is built on:

**1.** A limit is where the graph is heading, not the value at the point.
**2.** $x -> a^-$ means from the left, $x -> a^+$ means from the right.
**3.** The two-sided limit exists only when both sides agree. Otherwise it is DNE.

The two drills are open. Do them in either order.

theory.title: Theory drill
theory.blurb: True or false, multiple choice, fill in the blank

questions.explain: The limit says where the graph is heading. $f(3)$ could be 7, another number, or undefined.

questions.text: A function can have a limit at $x = a$ even if $f(a)$ is undefined.
questions.explain: A graph with an open circle still heads toward that height from both sides.

questions.text: If the left-hand and right-hand limits at $x = a$ are different numbers, the two-sided limit does not exist.
questions.explain: The two-sided limit needs both sides to agree.

questions.text: Changing the value of $f(2)$ changes $lim[x->2] f(x)$.
questions.explain: The limit only depends on the values of $f$ near 2, not at 2.

options: $f(x)$ gets close to $L$ as $x$ gets close to $a$ from both sides
questions.explain: A limit describes the height the outputs approach as the inputs approach $a$.

options: from the left, through values less than 4
from the right, through values greater than 4
questions.explain: The small minus sign means from the left side, where $x$ is less than 4.

questions.text: $lim[x->1^-] f(x) = 2$ and $lim[x->1^+] f(x) = 5$. What is $lim[x->1] f(x)$?
questions.explain: The sides disagree, so the two-sided limit does not exist. We never average them.

questions.text: $lim[x->1^-] f(x) = 4$ and $lim[x->1^+] f(x) = 4$, but $f(1) = 9$. What is $lim[x->1] f(x)$?
questions.explain: Both sides head to 4. The value $f(1) = 9$ does not affect the limit.

questions.text: A limit describes the height the graph is ___ as $x$ gets close to $a$, whether or not the function actually ___ it.
questions.explain: That is the whole idea of a limit.

questions.text: In $x -> a^-$, $x$ approaches $a$ from the ___. In $x -> a^+$, $x$ approaches $a$ from the ___.
questions.explain: Minus means from the left (smaller values). Plus means from the right (larger values).

questions.text: If $f(5)$ is undefined, then $lim[x->5] f(x)$ does not exist.
questions.explain: A hole in the graph does not stop the graph from heading toward a height.

questions.text: Which of these is NOT needed to find $lim[x->2] f(x)$?
options: The values of $f$ just to the left of 2
The values of $f$ just to the right of 2
questions.explain: The limit looks at values near 2 on both sides and ignores what happens exactly at 2.

questions.text: A one-sided limit can exist even when the two-sided limit does not.
questions.explain: At a jump, each side heads to its own height. Both one-sided limits exist, but they disagree.

questions.text: If a graph has only an open circle above $x = 3$, then $f(3)$ is ___, but the limit as $x$ approaches 3 can still ___.
questions.explain: No value at the point, but the graph still heads toward the open circle.

questions.text: The two-sided limit exists only when the two one-sided limits are ___. Otherwise the limit ___.
questions.explain: Agreement of the two sides is the test for a two-sided limit.
